html:
1The PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

Item Detail
Purpose Describe the expectations we have of ourselves and fellow practitioners: the ideals we aspire to and the behaviors that are mandatory; build confidence in the profession; help practitioners make wise decisions, especially when pressed to compromise integrity or values
Applies to All PMI members, and non-members who hold a PMI certification (such as PMP), apply for a PMI certification, or volunteer for PMI. One code for everyone
Four values Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, Honesty (identified by the global PM community as most important)
Aspirational standards The conduct we strive to uphold. Hard to measure, but not optional
Mandatory standards Firm requirements; some limit or prohibit behavior. Violations are subject to disciplinary procedures before PMI's Ethics Review Committee
Comments Examples and clarification; not mandatory parts of the Code

One act can breach both aspirational and mandatory standards.

Some bullets below come from the Code's comments (for example the list of illegal behaviors, the point about knowingly false allegations, and "treat the appearance of a conflict as a conflict"). Comments clarify the numbered standards rather than adding separate requirements, but exam questions treat them as expected conduct.

2Responsibility

Duty to take ownership for decisions we make or fail to make, actions we take or fail to take, and the consequences.

Aspirational

  • Decide and act in the best interests of society, public safety and the environment.
  • Accept only assignments consistent with your background, experience, skills and qualifications. For a developmental or stretch assignment, make sure key stakeholders get timely, complete information about your gaps so they can decide. In contracting, bid only on work your organization is qualified to perform and assign qualified people.
  • Fulfill commitments: do what you say you will do.
  • Own errors and omissions and correct them promptly; report others' errors to the appropriate body as soon as discovered; accept accountability for the consequences.
  • Protect proprietary or confidential information entrusted to you.
  • Uphold the Code and hold each other accountable.

Mandatory

  • Inform yourself of and uphold the policies, rules, regulations and laws governing your work.
  • Report unethical or illegal conduct to appropriate management and, if necessary, to those affected. Illegal behavior includes theft, fraud, corruption, embezzlement and bribery; also taking or abusing others' property including intellectual property, slander and libel. Do not condone or assist others in illegal behavior.
  • Bring Code violations to the attention of the appropriate body.
  • File ethics complaints only when substantiated by facts; do not accuse without all the facts; pursue action against knowingly false allegations.
  • Pursue disciplinary action against anyone who retaliates against a person raising ethics concerns.

3Respect

Duty to show a high regard for ourselves, others and the resources entrusted to us (people, money, reputation, safety, natural and environmental resources). An environment of respect builds trust, confidence and performance.

Aspirational

  • Learn the norms and customs of others and avoid behavior they would consider disrespectful.
  • Listen to others' points of view, seeking to understand.
  • Approach directly the people you have a conflict or disagreement with.
  • Stay professional even when it is not reciprocated. Avoid gossip and negative remarks that undermine others' reputations, and confront others who do so.

Mandatory

  • Negotiate in good faith.
  • Do not use the power of your expertise or position to influence decisions or actions to benefit yourself at others' expense.
  • Do not act in an abusive manner (conduct causing physical harm or intense fear, humiliation, manipulation or exploitation).
  • Respect the property rights of others.

4Fairness

Duty to make decisions and act impartially and objectively. Conduct must be free from competing self-interest, prejudice and favoritism.

Aspirational

  • Show transparency in the decision-making process.
  • Keep re-examining your impartiality and objectivity and take corrective action.
  • Actively look for potential conflicts of interest (one of the most challenging issues in practice) and help each other spot them.
  • Provide equal access to information to those authorized to have it (in bidding, equal information to all bidders).
  • Make opportunities equally available to qualified candidates.

Mandatory

  • Proactively and fully disclose real or potential conflicts of interest to the appropriate stakeholders.
  • On realizing a conflict, refrain from the decision-making process and from influencing outcomes until you have made full disclosure, have an approved mitigation plan, and have the consent of the stakeholders to proceed. Treat the appearance of a conflict as a conflict.
  • Do not hire or fire, reward or punish, or award or deny contracts on personal considerations (favoritism, nepotism, bribery).
  • Do not discriminate (gender, race, age, religion, disability, nationality, sexual orientation, etc.).
  • Apply organizational rules without favoritism or prejudice.

5Honesty

Duty to understand the truth and act truthfully in communication and conduct.

Aspirational

  • Earnestly seek the truth; be truthful in communications and conduct.
  • Provide accurate information in a timely manner; ensure the information behind decisions is accurate, reliable and timely.
  • Have the courage to share bad news even when it may be poorly received. When outcomes are negative, avoid burying information or shifting blame; when positive, avoid taking credit for others' achievements.
  • Make commitments and promises in good faith.
  • Create an environment in which others feel safe to tell the truth.

Mandatory

  • Do not engage in or condone deception: no false or misleading statements, half-truths, information out of context, or withholding information that would make statements misleading. Half-truths and non-disclosures intended to mislead are as unprofessional as outright misrepresentation.
  • No dishonest behavior for personal gain or at another's expense.

6Ethics in PMBOK 8

Where What it says
Accountable leader (Standard §3.6) Integrity, honesty and fairness are required of all team members; leaders demonstrate responsibility, respect, fairness and honesty and foster psychological safety; decisions focus on the common good and build trust
Integrity in the Resources domain (§2.6.3) Integrity = ethical behavior and honesty: share risks; communicate assumptions and the basis of estimates; deliver bad news early; make status reports an accurate picture of progress. Ethical behavior also includes spotlighting potential defects or negative effects in product design, disclosing potential conflicts of interest, ensuring fairness, and deciding on environmental, stakeholder and financial impacts
Respect and positive discourse Respect each person's thinking and skills; prefer dialogue (resolve divergent opinions) over debate (win-lose); transparency about biases builds openness and trust
Governance (§2.1) Governance frameworks align with ethical principles; project governance defines ethics and policies via OPAs
EEFs Organizational culture includes ethics and codes of conduct; social and cultural influences include ethics and perceptions
Risk (§2.7 and Table 4-2) Ethical risks and reputation, morale and other intangible risks may not fit the numeric scales; handle them with judgment
Procurement (Appendix X4.9) When handling claims and disputes: nuanced communication (emails can be evidence), clear escalation protocols, strict confidentiality, impartiality (facts over emotion)
AI (Appendix X3) Ethical risks of AI: bias, privacy, accountability; a human stays accountable for each decision (Topic 08)

7A Practical Approach to Ethical Dilemmas

Beyond PMBOK 8exam practice The "PMI answer" typically:

  • Complies with law and the Code first, even against pressure from a boss, customer or local custom.
  • Discloses (conflicts of interest, gaps in qualifications, errors) rather than hiding.
  • Refuses improper requests (bribes, falsified status or hours, misuse of confidential information).
  • Reports violations to the appropriate body or management instead of ignoring them, but only on facts.
  • Protects confidential information and people who raise concerns.
  • Stays direct and professional with the person involved (respect), without gossip.
Situation Best response
A vendor offers a lavish gift during bid evaluation Decline, and follow policy (report the offer where required); do not let it influence the decision
A relative's company is bidding Disclose the conflict, step out of the selection decision until a mitigation plan is approved and stakeholders consent
A sponsor asks to report "green" on a late project Report accurately with the facts and a recovery plan
You discover your own estimating or billing error Own it and correct it promptly; inform affected parties
A request for a competitor's confidential data Refuse; protect confidentiality
Asked to lead work beyond your experience Disclose the gaps to key stakeholders so they can decide
A local partner demands a "facilitation payment" Refuse; it is bribery or illegal; take it to legal and compliance; custom is not an excuse
A team member uses pirated or unlicensed software Stop it and report to appropriate management (intellectual property, law)
A colleague reports discriminatory behavior Take it to the appropriate body; protect the reporter from retaliation; keep it factual
A defect or safety risk would embarrass the sponsor Share it early and factually; protect public safety and stakeholders

8Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Ethics is approach-neutral; the expression differs.

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Transparency Accurate status reports, baselines, change logs Information radiators, honest burn charts, open reviews Both
Honesty about progress No "watermelon" reports (green outside, red inside) Report true velocity and impediments; no inflating story points Consistent truth across streams
Fairness Fair bid process and equal information to bidders Fair prioritization; no favoritism in backlog ordering Both
Psychological safety Safe to raise issues at gates Safe to speak up in retrospectives Both

9Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Truth over comfort. Never misreport status, hours, quality or risks to please someone. Share bad news early with facts and options.
  2. Disclose conflicts, then step back. Disclosure alone is not enough: refrain from deciding until mitigation is approved and stakeholders consent.
  3. Law and the Code beat local custom and pressure. Do not pay bribes or "facilitation payments" even if customary; seek legal and compliance guidance.
  4. Report, but on facts. Report illegal or unethical conduct to the appropriate body; do not make unsubstantiated accusations or gossip.
  5. Protect confidentiality and intellectual property; do not use information from another client or employer.
  6. Own your mistakes promptly instead of hiding or blaming.
  7. Do not retaliate; protect those who raise concerns.
  8. Be honest about your qualifications and gaps.
  9. Fair process in procurement and hiring: equal access to information, no favoritism or nepotism.
  10. Go to the person first (respect), then the proper channel if the issue is serious or unresolved.
  11. When the options are "ignore", "do it quietly" or "escalate through the right channel", the right channel is usually correct, after you have the facts.
  12. Ethics in newer areas: AI (bias, privacy, accountability), sustainability (honesty about environmental claims), data protection.

10Exam Q&A

10.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1During a tender, a bidder's representative phones the project manager to ask which price range the other bidders submitted, hinting at future business in return. What should the project manager do?

  • AGive only the general price range, as the exact bidder figures stay confidential until award
  • BAnswer the questions in writing for that bidder and for no other bidder
  • CDecline to share anything, treat bidders equally and report the approach under policy
  • DIgnore the call and mention it to no one, as nothing was agreed
Show the answer

Answer: C. Fairness requires equal access to information for all bidders, and hints of future business in exchange for information are improper influence that is reported under policy. Sharing any part of it, answering one bidder alone or staying silent breaches fairness or the duty to report.

S2The project manager discovers that her brother-in-law owns one of the companies bidding on a contract she helps evaluate. What should she do?

  • AAsk her brother-in-law to withdraw his company's bid from the process
  • BEvaluate that bid last so that it cannot influence her other scores
  • CSay nothing, because she is confident that she can evaluate it fairly
  • DDisclose the relationship and step out of the evaluation until it is resolved
Show the answer

Answer: D. Real or apparent conflicts of interest must be disclosed, and the person refrains from the decision until a mitigation plan is approved and the stakeholders consent. Confidence in one's own fairness, pressuring the bidder or reordering the work does not remove the conflict.

S3A sponsor under pressure asks the project manager to report the release as "on track" although the product team is three weeks behind its release plan. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the PMO to submit the status report in the project's place
  • BReport on track now and hope the team recovers the three weeks
  • CReport the true status with the causes and a recovery plan
  • DDelay the status report until the lost time has been recovered
Show the answer

Answer: C. Honesty requires accurate, timely information and the courage to share bad news, together with a plan to recover. Misreporting, delaying or handing the report to someone else all avoid the responsibility.

S4On a hybrid ERP project billed on a time-and-materials basis, the project manager realizes that an estimating error caused hours to be over-billed to the customer for two months. What should she do?

  • AWait to see whether the customer notices the difference first
  • BTake ownership, correct the error and tell the customer promptly
  • CAdjust the next invoices quietly so that the overall total evens out over time
  • DBlame the timekeeping system and ask the vendor for a fix
Show the answer

Answer: B. Responsibility means owning errors, correcting them promptly and informing those affected. Quiet adjustments, waiting or blaming a tool hide the error from the customer.

S5A customer representative asks the project manager for pricing details from a competitor's earlier project that the project manager worked on. What should she do?

  • ADecline, citing the confidentiality obligations she still holds
  • BShare the figures because the earlier project has been completed
  • CShare the figures if the customer promises to keep them secret
  • DShare a summary of the prices that leaves out the competitor's name
Show the answer

Answer: A. Protecting confidential and proprietary information is a duty that continues after a project ends. Anonymizing the data, accepting a promise of secrecy or relying on completion does not release it.

S6A manager asks the project manager to lead a hybrid program that uses a technology she has never worked with. She is interested but lacks the experience. What is the best action?

  • AAccept the role and delegate all technical questions to hide the gap
  • BAccept without comment and learn the technology while leading
  • CDecline the assignment without giving the manager any explanation
  • DAccept after telling key stakeholders about the gaps in her experience
Show the answer

Answer: D. For stretch assignments, key stakeholders must receive timely, complete information about the gaps so they can decide. Silence, a bare refusal or concealment by delegation withholds the facts.

S7In a country where small cash payments to officials are common, a local agent says a "facilitation fee" will speed up a required permit. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk a team member to arrange the payment informally on the side
  • BPay the fee but record it in the project accounts as consulting
  • CPay the fee because it is the local custom for such permits
  • DRefuse to pay and ask legal and compliance for a lawful route
Show the answer

Answer: D. Bribery is illegal and unethical, and custom is not an excuse; the project manager upholds the law and seeks a lawful route with legal and compliance support. Paying openly, disguising the payment or delegating it all take part in the same violation.

S8A team member tells the project manager that a lead engineer repeatedly makes discriminatory remarks about colleagues in the daily coordination meeting. What should the project manager do?

  • AReprimand the engineer in front of the whole team to set an example
  • BGather the facts and report to the proper body while protecting the reporter
  • CMove the reporting team member to another project to avoid friction
  • DIgnore it for now unless several more colleagues complain about the engineer
Show the answer

Answer: B. Discrimination breaches fairness and respect, so the matter goes to the appropriate body on the facts and the reporter is protected from retaliation. Ignoring it, a public reprimand or relocating the reporter all fail to follow that route.

S9A steering committee praises the project manager for a cost-saving method that a junior analyst actually designed. How should the project manager respond?

  • AThank the committee and state clearly that the junior analyst created the method
  • BDescribe the method as a joint effort so that nobody is singled out
  • CSay nothing, since the team's success also reflects well on the manager
  • DAccept the praise for now and credit the junior analyst later in the closing report
Show the answer

Answer: A. Honesty means not taking credit for others' achievements, so the project manager corrects the record at once. Accepting praise first, staying silent or blurring the credit leaves a false impression with the committee.

S10A tester on an agile team finds a defect that could affect user safety. The sponsor wants to delay telling the customer until after a launch event. What should the project manager do?

  • AWait until after the launch event, as the sponsor has requested
  • BTell only the project team so that the sponsor's plan is kept
  • CInform the right stakeholders promptly with the facts and a mitigation plan
  • DFix the defect quietly in the next build and say nothing to the customer afterward
Show the answer

Answer: C. Public safety comes first, and honesty requires timely disclosure of the facts with a mitigation plan. Waiting, fixing quietly or limiting the circle conceals a risk to users.

10.2 Recall Q&As

R1What are the four values of the PMI Code?

Show the answer

Responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty.

R2What is the difference between aspirational and mandatory standards?

Show the answer

Aspirational standards describe conduct we strive for (not optional); mandatory standards are firm requirements, and breaches lead to disciplinary procedures.

R3Who must follow the Code?

Show the answer

PMI members, non-members holding a PMI certification, those applying for certification, and PMI volunteers.

R4What must you do when you have a conflict of interest?

Show the answer

Disclose it, and refrain from decisions or influence until you have disclosed fully, have an approved mitigation plan and have stakeholder consent. Treat the appearance of a conflict as a conflict.

R5What does honesty require when news is bad?

Show the answer

Courage to share it; do not bury information or shift blame; provide accurate, timely information.

R6What is required about laws and rules?

Show the answer

Inform yourself of and uphold the policies, rules, regulations and laws governing your work; report illegal or unethical conduct.

R7What is the limit on ethics complaints?

Show the answer

File only when substantiated by facts; avoid unfounded accusations.

R8What does fairness require about information in bidding?

Show the answer

Equal access to information for those authorized, and equal opportunities for qualified candidates.

R9What does PMBOK 8 list as honest behavior for project managers?

Show the answer

Sharing risks, communicating assumptions and estimate bases, delivering bad news early, and accurate status reports.

R10What are the ethical concerns PMBOK 8 raises for AI?

Show the answer

Bias, privacy, accountability.

R11What should you do before accepting a stretch assignment?

Show the answer

Make sure key stakeholders receive timely and complete information about your qualification gaps.

R12What is respect's rule about negotiation and power?

Show the answer

Negotiate in good faith, and do not use your expertise or position to benefit yourself at others' expense.

11Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Code values Responsibility · Respect · Fairness · Honesty
Standards Aspirational (strive) and mandatory (must; discipline)
Applies to PMI members, certification holders and applicants, PMI volunteers
Responsibility Own decisions and errors; accept suitable assignments; protect confidentiality; uphold law; report violations
Respect Understand norms; listen; address conflict directly; negotiate in good faith; no abuse of power
Fairness Transparency; equal access; disclose conflicts and recuse until mitigation + consent; no favoritism or discrimination
Honesty Truthful, accurate, timely; courage with bad news; no half-truths or misleading omissions
Conflict of interest Disclose → step back → approved mitigation plan → stakeholder consent
PMBOK 8 integrity Share risks, state assumptions, bad news early, accurate status
Claims and disputes Careful wording, escalation protocol, confidentiality, impartiality
AI ethics Bias, privacy, accountability
First-action pattern Get the facts, check law/policy/Code, disclose or refuse, report through the right channel, protect people
